title: My soul thirsteth (Psalm 62 [63])
hookLine: the Sunday morning psalm: early I seek thee in a dry land

lines: THE FIRST THING YOU REACH FOR.
THE FIRST MINUTE OF THE DAY.
cards: What's the first thing you reach for in the morning? For most people it's the phone, before the eyes are fully open: messages, news, the weather, somebody's vacation photos.
The first minute of the day goes to whatever is loudest. An old Christian habit gives that minute to something else.
For centuries, monks and nuns greeted the first light with one particular psalm, a song that starts with a person awake early, thirsty, in a dry place.

teach.h: TO THEE DO I WATCH AT BREAK OF DAY.
teach.b: Psalm 62 in the Douay, 63 in most Bibles. Its heading places David in the desert, far from the sanctuary. The Douay begins: "O God, my God, to thee do I watch at break of day."
The Hebrew verb comes from the word for dawn: I seek you at first light. That's why many English Bibles say early will I seek thee.

teach.h: A DRY LAND WITH NO WATER.
teach.b: Then the thirst: my soul thirsts for you, my flesh longs for you, like a dry, weary land where there is no water. Not just the soul; the body too. Then a line that stops people: "For thy mercy is better than lives."

teach.h: THY MERCY IS BETTER THAN LIVES.
teach.b: Better than life itself, better than any number of lives. Then the night. If I have remembered you on my bed, the psalm says, I will think of you in the morning.
The one praying has been awake in the dark, and wakes still turned toward God.

teach.h: MY SOUL HATH STUCK CLOSE TO THEE.
teach.b: It ends with closeness so physical it's almost a hug: "My soul hath stuck close to thee: thy right hand hath received me." Clinging, the way a child holds a parent's leg.

Saint John Chrysostom, in the fourth century, said the fathers before him had appointed it to be sung every morning. Today in the Liturgy of the Hours it opens Morning Prayer on Sundays and on great feasts.
The first minute of the day, given to thirst.

how: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say Psalm 62 [63] at Morning Prayer on Sundays and on feasts; it has been treated as the Church's morning psalm since at least the fourth century.

o: Hebrew for dawn, hidden in seek you early
Hebrew for thirst, as in a dry, weary land
Hebrew for the desert where David hid

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: when the psalmist watches for God

s: this psalm has long been sung in the morning
Chrysostom said the fathers had appointed it for every morning; today it opens Sunday Morning Prayer.
the psalm speaks only of the soul, not the body
my soul thirsts, and my flesh longs too, like a dry land.
the psalm says God's mercy is better than lives
lives, plural: better than life itself.

games.q: you wake up at dawn, thirsty, in the desert, on the run. what's the first thing the psalmist does?
o: turn to God: to thee do I watch at break of day.
games.why: O God, my God, to thee do I watch at break of day. the first thing he reaches for is God, and he says he's thirsty for him.

practice: Picture the moment you wake, eyes still heavy, the phone somewhere nearby, and before you touch it, one line: O God, my God, to thee do I watch at break of day. Say it now, three times, slowly, so it's ready for the morning.
If you pray, let it be your first word to God tomorrow; if you don't, let it be a way of choosing what gets your first minute.

wordCard.voice: Shachar. Hebrew for dawn, the root of the morning psalm's seek you early, a person awake at first light, thirsty for God in a dry land. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: I seek you early, from shachar, dawn. the verb behind early will I seek thee.

carryVoice: Your line: early I seek you. Before the loudest thing gets there. That's day one hundred seventy-two.
